summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative obligation on a State to protect a child from private violence it did not create, even where the agency received repeated abuse reports and failed to act. (Joshua DeShaney was never in state custody and survived with profound brain injury; this is not a death-in-care case.)
key_cases.relevance: A screen-out that later proves catastrophic is not, without more, a federal constitutional violation.
key_cases.quote: its language cannot fairly be extended to impose an affirmative obligation on the State to ensure that those interests do not come to harm through other means.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Officials may not enter a home or seize a child without prior judicial authorization unless they possess information at the time of seizure establishing reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury, and the intrusion must be no broader than necessary to avert that injury.
key_cases.relevance: An uncorroborated allegation that fails this test is one the agency must investigate further rather than act on.
key_cases.quote: reasonable cause to believe that the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury and that the scope of the intrusion is reasonably necessary to avert that specific injury.

timeline_requirements.deadline: As part of an investigation initiated pursuant to NRS 432B.260 the agency must determine, first in the order of priority set by the rule, whether the child is safe considering the factors set forth in NAC 432B.160; no separate deadline is set for that determination (NAC 432B.150(2)). The child must be seen immediately if the allegations suggest imminent harm (NAC 432B.150(3)(b)), and where the investigation was initiated by telephone or a review of a case record a face-to-face meeting with the child and his family must be attempted on the next business day and on each successive business day until the supervisor of the case manager of the case determines that a resolution has been achieved (NAC 432B.155(1))
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Investigation initiated by the agency which provides child welfare services pursuant to NRS 432B.260
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in NAC 432B.150 or NAC 432B.155
